overview.title: Turn Tiny Shakespeare into character ids
overview.summary: Download the plays, treat each character as a token, and write the binaries and the codec training will read.

sections.title: Get the text and build a character codec
sections.pseudocode:
Download Tiny Shakespeare and write it to input.txt if it is not already there.
The sorted set of characters is the vocabulary. **stoi** and **itos** translate both ways.
# Insight: One character is one token. That is the whole difference from the GPT-2 tokenizer.

sections.title: Write train.bin, val.bin, and meta.pkl
sections.pseudocode:
Cut the text at 0.9. Encode both sides as uint16.
Save the binaries and a meta.pkl that holds the vocabulary and both maps.
# Insight: train.py reads the bins. sample.py reads meta.pkl so letters survive the round trip.

logic.title: Turn Tiny Shakespeare into character ids
logic.summary: Download the play text if needed, map each character to an integer, and write train and validation binaries.

sections.title: Download the text if it is not here yet
sections.pseudocode:
Look for input.txt next to this script.
If it is missing, download the Tiny Shakespeare file.
Write that download to input.txt.
# Context: The file is the same tiny corpus char-rnn used. One download is enough; later runs reuse input.txt.

sections.title: Let the characters themselves be the vocabulary
sections.pseudocode:
Read the whole file as one string.
Print how many characters that is.
Sort the distinct characters. That list is the vocabulary.
Print them, and print **vocab_size**.
Map each character to its index. Call that **stoi**.
Map each index back to its character. Call that **itos**.
Encoding walks the string and replaces each character.
Decoding joins the characters for those ids.
# Insight: There is no byte-pair merge here. A token is one character, so the model's vocabulary is the alphabet, about 65 symbols in this text.
# Context: stoi and itos are inverses. sample.py reads both from meta.pkl so it can prompt and print in letters, not ids.

sections.title: Save a 90/10 split as uint16 binaries
sections.pseudocode:
Put the first 90% of the characters in train.
Put the last 10% in validation.
The cut is at 0.9 of the length.
Encode both strings to id lists.
Print both lengths.
Store the ids as uint16.
Write train.bin and val.bin next to this script.
Save **vocab_size**, **itos**, and **stoi** in meta.pkl.
# Why: uint16 is enough for a 65-character alphabet and matches the dtype train.py memory-maps.
# Insight: The split is a single cut in document order, not a shuffle. The validation tail is later text from the same file.
